summary:
Aksaray stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 of them recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality. It would criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch called the draft one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it. The measure had not been passed when reported, but authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at its launch, documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy under a Year of the Family banner, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between pending legislation and practice. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafes in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for General Information Gathering background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her.

Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, and Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk for a visitor whose appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

The surviving record for this province is entirely national-level and carries no Aksaray-specific breakdown. Neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established from the inventory, and the documented national picture applies here unchanged.
tangentialFactors:
Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

The Erdoğan government frames its position as protecting the family and public morals, language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. The pending status of the draft package has not prevented enforcement from preceding legislation, a pattern the detained woman in Istanbul described directly.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Transition-related care is tightening for residents. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added gender reassignment as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the other option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025 and confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison, with custody conditions for trans prisoners under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses Aksaray directly. The absence of provincial material is a gap in sourcing, not a finding that conditions in Aksaray differ from the national record; local police practice, municipal services and any provincial health-directorate circulars specific to Aksaray remain unresolved.

The 11th Judicial Package was reported as a leaked draft and had not been passed as of October 2025. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is not sourced here and should be rechecked against current legislation before travel.

The claim that street-level GBT checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights rests on legal experts cited in reporting rather than on a court ruling; no judgment establishing that position is sourced in the inventory.

Figures on detentions and violations come from Kaos GL's own monitoring and may undercount incidents that never reached formal channels, as the 43 off-record detention decisions suggest.
